ask.changes_what: New orthopnoea raises probability of decompensated HF and supports BNP/echo and decongestion; absence should not be used to exclude HF.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on the absence of orthopnoea to exclude heart failure, and do not attribute orthopnoea to heart failure without examining for tamponade, effusion or neuromuscular weakness when the picture does not fit.
ask.escalation_warning: Orthopnoea with hypotension, pulsus paradoxus or a raised JVP suggests tamponade or acute pump failure; obtain immediate echo.

evidence.citation: Fonseca C, Morais H, Mota T, et al. The diagnosis of heart failure in primary care: value of symptoms and signs. Eur J Heart Fail. 2004;6(6):795-800.

evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (cardiac dysfunction at rest on echocardiography)

evidence.reference_standard: Centrally adjudicated definite heart failure (CHS criteria)
evidence.target_condition: Prevalent definite heart failure (composite symptom: orthopnoea OR paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)

ask.how: Ask whether breathing worsens within minutes of lying flat and eases on sitting up, how many pillows (or what head-of-bed angle) are needed to sleep, and whether this is new or increased compared with baseline. Distinguish from positional dyspnoea due to abdominal distension, obesity, or nasal obstruction, and from cough-related waking.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of orthopnoea only modestly lowers the probability of heart failure; many heart failure patients, particularly with chronic disease, sleep flat.
ask.pitfalls: Orthopnoea also occurs with COPD, massive ascites, obesity, and bilateral diaphragm paralysis; pillow count is confounded by habit, reflux and sinus disease. In chronic HF orthopnoea correlates poorly with measured wedge pressure.
ask.positive_finding: New or worsening need to sleep propped up, with dyspnoea on lying flat that resolves on sitting, points to raised left-sided filling pressure (heart failure) or, less often, tamponade, large effusion or bilateral diaphragm weakness.
ask.prerequisites: Patient (or collateral historian) able to describe sleep position and recent change.
ask.rationale: Orthopnea is a classic symptom of acute decompensated heart failure and would strongly support that diagnosis in this patient with overnight dyspnea.
ask.title: Orthopnea: dyspnea lying flat relieved by sitting up / number of pillows

ask.changes_what: PND raises probability of decompensated HF (pooled LR+ ~2.6 in ED) and supports BNP/echo; absence changes little.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of PND to exclude heart failure; do not label nocturnal wheeze as asthma in an older patient with risk factors for heart failure without checking for congestion.
ask.escalation_warning: PND with chest pain, new oedema or hypoxaemia at rest indicates decompensation that needs same-day assessment rather than outpatient follow-up.

ask.how: Ask whether the patient wakes from sleep, typically 1-3 hours after lying down, gasping or short of breath and has to sit up, stand or go to a window for relief that takes 10-30 minutes. Ask about wheeze or cough with the episodes and about daytime exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea and oedema to separate cardiac from asthmatic nocturnal symptoms.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of PND is common in heart failure and provides little reassurance; it should not lower the probability enough to stop the work-up.
ask.pitfalls: Nocturnal asthma, COPD with secretions, sleep apnoea, reflux/aspiration and nocturnal angina produce similar waking; 'cardiac asthma' with wheeze is easily mislabelled as asthma. Recall is unreliable and prevalence is low so specificity drives its value.
ask.positive_finding: Episodes of waking from sleep with dyspnoea that resolve slowly on sitting or standing indicate redistribution of fluid into the lungs from raised left-sided filling pressure, i.e. decompensated heart failure.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or bed partner able to describe nocturnal episodes.
ask.rationale: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is highly suggestive of heart failure and would prompt early diuresis and cardiac workup if present.
ask.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: waking 1-3 h after sleep with dyspnea relieved by sitting/standing

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: VTE risk factors are important to assess for pulmonary embolism, which is a key alternative diagnosis in acute hypoxemic dyspnea.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: Elevated JVP moves dyspnea/edema toward acute HF or RV/pericardial disease and away from hypovolemia; a flat JVP in hypotension favors hypovolemia/sepsis over cardiogenic causes.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm neck pressure in patients with carotid disease.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal JVP to withhold treatment for suspected heart failure, or declare a shocked patient hypovolemic when the neck cannot be adequately examined (obesity, short neck, column above the jaw).
examine.escalation_warning: Elevated JVP with hypotension, clear lungs and tachycardia suggests tamponade, RV infarction or massive PE and needs immediate echo/POCUS rather than diuresis.

evidence.citation: Butman SM, Ewy GA, Standen JR, Kern KB, Hahn E. Bedside cardiovascular examination in patients with severe chronic heart failure: importance of rest or inducible jugular venous distension. J Am Coll Cardiol 1993;22(4):968-74.

evidence.quote: had the best combination of sensitivity (81%), specificity (80%) and predictive accuracy (81%) for elevation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
evidence.target_condition: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (>=18 mmHg)

evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of HF per included studies (varied)
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure as cause of acute dyspnea

evidence.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care

examine.how: Recline the patient at 30-45 degrees (adjust until the top of the pulsation is visible), turn the head slightly left, and use tangential light to find the top of the internal jugular column. Measure its vertical height above the sternal angle; >3 cm above the angle (about >8 cm H2O total) is elevated.
examine.negative_finding: A flat or normal JVP lowers but does not exclude heart failure; sensitivity is modest (roughly 0.2-0.7 across ED studies) and pooled sensitivity in ED series stays below 0.55.
examine.pitfalls: Confusing carotid with venous pulsation, misjudging the sternal angle-to-atrium distance (varies with position), and failing to see a very high column (look for earlobe pulsation) or a very low one (lie the patient flatter). Isolated RV failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade or constriction raise JVP without left-sided congestion.
examine.positive_finding: A venous column >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised right atrial pressure and, in chronic heart failure, usually raised left-sided filling pressure (PCWP >=18 mmHg). It substantially raises the probability of heart failure as the cause of acute dyspnea.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate light, exposed neck, patient relaxed and breathing quietly; identify the venous (biphasic, non-palpable, falls with inspiration, occludable) rather than carotid pulsation.
examine.rationale: Elevated JVP is a critical bedside sign of volume overload and supports acute heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.
examine.title: Jugular venous pressure elevated (>8 cm H2O / >3 cm above sternal angle); low/flat JVP as the negative

examine.changes_what: Bibasilar crackles favor HF (add JVP, S3, BNP/POCUS); focal crackles with fever favor pneumonia (CXR); clear lungs do not rule out either but lower HF probability modestly.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use clear lungs to exclude heart failure in chronic HF patients (crackles are often absent with high filling pressures) or to exclude pneumonia in the elderly/immunocompromised, where auscultation is insensitive.
examine.escalation_warning: Diffuse crackles with hypoxemia and hypotension suggest pulmonary edema from cardiogenic shock or ARDS and require immediate escalation regardless of etiology.

evidence.quote: rales (negative LR = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.37-0.70)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/echo-based HF diagnosis per included studies
evidence.target_condition: Congestive heart failure as cause of dyspnea (absence of rales)

evidence.target_condition: Radiographic community-acquired pneumonia (crackles present)

evidence.citation: Marchello CS, Ebell MH, Dale AP, Harvill ET, Shen Y, Whalen CC. Signs and symptoms that rule out community-acquired pneumonia in outpatient adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Am Board Fam Med 2019;32(2):234-47.
evidence.population: Outpatient adults/adolescents with acute respiratory infection; 3 studies; baseline CAP risk ~4%
evidence.quote: had a summary estimate of LR- of 0.10 (95% CI, 0.07 to 0.13) with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.92
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia; COMPOSITE rule-out = normal vital signs AND normal pulmonary examination (no crackles or other auscultatory abnormality)

examine.how: With the patient sitting, auscultate posterior bases and all fields during slow deep breaths through an open mouth, comparing sides. Have the patient cough before calling crackles persistent; note timing (late-inspiratory fine = edema/fibrosis; coarse = secretions), distribution (bibasilar symmetric vs focal), and whether they clear with position change.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of crackles lowers the probability of heart failure only moderately (LR- 0.35-0.51) and does not exclude pneumonia; normal vital signs plus a normal lung examination together make CAP unlikely (LR- 0.10).
examine.pitfalls: Dependent-atelectasis crackles clear with deep breaths or cough; chronic 'velcro' crackles of fibrosis mimic edema; in chronic HF crackles are often absent despite high wedge pressure, and obese or shallow-breathing patients give false negatives.
examine.positive_finding: Bibasilar symmetric late-inspiratory crackles in an acutely dyspneic adult raise the probability of heart failure (pooled specificity ~0.77-0.81); focal/unilateral crackles with fever or cough raise the probability of pneumonia (pooled LR+ ~2.4). Crackles are non-specific and also occur in ILD, atelectasis, COPD and bronchiectasis.
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, diaphragm on skin, patient able to take deep breaths; re-listen after several deep breaths because dependent atelectasis crackles clear.
examine.rationale: Bibasilar crackles point toward heart failure, while focal crackles suggest pneumonia, helping to distinguish between leading causes.
examine.title: Pulmonary crackles: bibasilar (heart failure) vs focal/unilateral (pneumonia)

examine.changes_what: Present: escalate now (continuous monitoring, blood gas, bronchodilator/NIV or airway plan). Absent: do not use to downgrade severity; rely on oximetry, gas and peak flow.
examine.contraindications: None; it is observation only. Do not delay oxygen, bronchodilator or airway management to complete the assessment.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of the sign to withhold escalation in a drowsy, exhausted or silent-chest patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Accessory muscle use plus inability to speak, drowsiness, silent chest, bradycardia or SpO2 <90% = life-threatening exacerbation: immediate senior/ICU involvement.
examine.how: Observe from the doorway before touching the patient: sternocleidomastoid/scalene contraction on inspiration, suprasternal or intercostal retraction, tripod posture, pursed-lip exhalation, and diaphoresis. Ask an open question and note whether the patient can finish a sentence in one breath (sentences vs phrases vs single words).
examine.negative_finding: Absence of accessory muscle use does not exclude significant airflow limitation or hypercapnia; a tiring or obtunded patient may lose the sign as ventilatory failure develops.
examine.pitfalls: Loss of accessory muscle use with rising drowsiness signals fatigue, not improvement. Obesity, a thick neck and supine positioning hide sternocleidomastoid contraction.
examine.positive_finding: Visible accessory muscle use, tripoding or speech limited to words/phrases marks a severe exacerbation of airflow obstruction (asthma/COPD) or another cause of high work of breathing, and in admitted asthmatics is associated with a markedly lower %FEV1. Treat it as a severity marker, not as a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Patient undressed enough to see the neck and chest wall; observe at rest before any intervention if safe to do so.
examine.rationale: Visible work of breathing indicates severity and need for urgent escalation, regardless of the underlying cause.
examine.title: Work of breathing: accessory muscle use, tripoding, pursed-lip breathing, inability to speak full sentences

examine.changes_what: Dullness + reduced fremitus: order CXR/POCUS for effusion. Dullness + increased fremitus/egophony: treat as consolidation. Normal fremitus at low pretest probability: may skip imaging.
examine.do_not_use_when: Not a substitute for imaging when effusion or empyema would change management (e.g., febrile patient with suspected parapneumonic effusion).
examine.escalation_warning: Dullness with fever and hypoxia or with unilateral absent breath sounds and hemodynamic compromise warrants urgent imaging and drainage assessment.

evidence.quote: dullness to conventional percussion was most accurate for diagnosing pleural effusion (summary positive likelihood ratio, 8.7; 95% confidence interval, 2.2-33.8)
evidence.target_condition: Pleural effusion (dullness to conventional percussion)

evidence.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.

evidence.target_condition: Pleural effusion (absence of reduced tactile vocal fremitus)

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
evidence.quote: dullness to percussion (LR+ = 2.62, 95% CI = 1.14 to 5.30)
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (dullness to percussion)

examine.how: Patient sitting; percuss the posterior and lateral chest from apex to base, comparing sides at each level, and mark where resonance changes to dull. Then ask the patient to say 'ninety-nine' while palpating the same sites with the ulnar hand edge to grade tactile fremitus. Auscultatory percussion: tap the manubrium while listening over the posterior chest.
examine.negative_finding: Normal (non-reduced) tactile fremitus lowers the probability of effusion (LR- 0.21) and may make radiography unnecessary when pretest probability is low.
examine.pitfalls: Small effusions (<300-500 mL) are missed; obesity, raised hemidiaphragm, and dense consolidation all produce dullness. Conventional percussion outperforms auscultatory percussion in pooled data.
examine.positive_finding: Stony dullness with reduced fremitus over a base strongly favors pleural effusion (pooled LR+ 8.7); dullness with increased fremitus and bronchial breathing favors consolidation (LR+ 2.6 for CAP).
examine.prerequisites: Bare skin, patient able to sit or lie lateral, quiet room.
examine.rationale: Dullness to percussion can help identify pleural effusion or consolidation, which are important alternative causes of acute dyspnea.
examine.title: Dullness to percussion with decreased tactile fremitus (focal; conventional vs auscultatory percussion)

Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is highly suggestive of heart failure and would prompt early diuresis and cardiac workup if present.
VTE risk factors are important to assess for pulmonary embolism, which is a key alternative diagnosis in acute hypoxemic dyspnea.

examine.rationale: Elevated JVP is a critical bedside sign of volume overload and supports acute heart failure as the cause of dyspnea.
Bibasilar crackles point toward heart failure, while focal crackles suggest pneumonia, helping to distinguish between leading causes.
Visible work of breathing indicates severity and need for urgent escalation, regardless of the underlying cause.
Dullness to percussion can help identify pleural effusion or consolidation, which are important alternative causes of acute dyspnea.
